translations.title: Create Scaled Picture Graphs
translations.explanation: Create Scaled Picture Graphs is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Introducing Multiplication”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:3.MD.B.3. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Draw a scaled picture graph and a scaled bar graph to represent a data set with several categories. Solve one- and two-step “how many more” and “how many less” problems using information presented in scaled bar graphs. For example, draw a bar graph in which each square in the bar graph might represent 5 pets. Instructional focus: Students connect measurable attributes with units, measurement procedures, representations of data, and calculations that answer a concrete question. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Create Scaled Picture Graphs. Choose a unit that matches the attribute, use equal-size units without gaps or overlaps, record the unit with the number, and interpret tables, line plots, clocks, money, area, volume, or angle measures according to the problem.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: A rectangle measures 10 units by 7 units. Its area is 10 × 7 = 70 square units, while its perimeter is 2(10+7) = 34 units. Example 2: A rectangle measures 5 units by 4 units. Its area is 5 × 4 = 20 square units, while its perimeter is 2(5+4) = 18 units.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify the requested attribute and units. Step 2: for area, multiply length by width: 10×7=70. Step 3: for perimeter, add all side lengths: 2(10+7)=34. Step 4: attach square units to area and linear units to perimeter. Step 1: identify the requested attribute and units. Step 2: for area, multiply length by width: 5×4=20. Step 3: for perimeter, add all side lengths: 2(5+4)=18. Step 4: attach square units to area and linear units to perimeter.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Create Scaled Picture Graphs. A number without its unit can be incomplete. Do not mix incompatible units before converting them. In graphs, read the scale and labels before drawing conclusions; in geometric measurement, distinguish length, area, angle, and volume.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Create Scaled Picture Graphs. Identify what is measured, choose or convert units correctly, calculate or read the representation, and state the result with its unit and meaning.

translations.title: Create Scaled Picture Wykresy
translations.explanation: Lekcja „Create Scaled Picture Wykresy” należy do działu „Introducing Multiplication” i jest dokładnie powiązana ze standardami CCSS:3.MD.B.3. Główny kierunek pracy: Uczeń łączy mierzalne cechy z jednostkami, sposobem wykonywania pomiaru, reprezentacją danych i obliczeniami odpowiadającymi na konkretne pytanie. Tytuł i kolejność pochodzą z zaakceptowanego źródła pedagogicznego, natomiast granice merytoryczne wyznaczają oficjalne standardy Common Core.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Cel tej lekcji: Create Scaled Picture Wykresy. Dobierz jednostkę do mierzonej cechy, używaj jednostek jednakowej wielkości bez luk i nakładania, zapisuj jednostkę przy wyniku i interpretuj tabele, wykresy, czas, pieniądze, pole, objętość lub kąty zgodnie z zadaniem.
translations.workedExamples: Przykład 1: Prostokąt ma wymiary 10 na 7 jednostek. Pole wynosi 10 × 7 = 70 jednostek kwadratowych, a obwód 2(10+7) = 34 jednostek. Przykład 2: Prostokąt ma wymiary 5 na 4 jednostek. Pole wynosi 5 × 4 = 20 jednostek kwadratowych, a obwód 2(5+4) = 18 jednostek.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Krok 1: rozpoznaj mierzoną wielkość i jednostkę. Krok 2: pole: 10×7=70. Krok 3: obwód: 2(10+7)=34. Krok 4: przy polu zapisz jednostki kwadratowe, a przy obwodzie liniowe. Krok 1: rozpoznaj mierzoną wielkość i jednostkę. Krok 2: pole: 5×4=20. Krok 3: obwód: 2(5+4)=18. Krok 4: przy polu zapisz jednostki kwadratowe, a przy obwodzie liniowe.
translations.commonMistakes: Cel tej lekcji: Create Scaled Picture Wykresy. Liczba bez jednostki może być niepełną odpowiedzią. Nie łącz różnych jednostek bez przeliczenia. Na wykresie najpierw sprawdź skalę i opisy; w geometrii odróżniaj długość, pole, miarę kąta i objętość.
translations.quickSummary: Cel tej lekcji: Create Scaled Picture Wykresy. Ustal, co jest mierzone, prawidłowo dobierz lub przelicz jednostki, wykonaj obliczenie albo odczyt i podaj wynik z jednostką oraz znaczeniem.

translations.title: Multiplication as Equal Groups
translations.explanation: Multiplication as Equal Groups is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Introducing Multiplication”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:3.OA.A.1. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Interpret products of whole numbers, e.g., interpret 5 × 7 as the total number of objects in 5 groups of 7 objects each. For example, describe a context in which a total number of objects can be expressed as 5 × 7. Instructional focus: Students reason about equal groups, arrays, factors, products, quotients, and unknown group sizes. Multiplication and division are connected inverse relationships. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.

translations.title: The Commutative Property PLC Activity
translations.explanation: The Commutative Property PLC Activity is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Introducing Multiplication”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:3.OA.B.5. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide.2 Examples: If 6 × 4 = 24 is known, then 4 × 6 = 24 is also known. (Commutative property of multiplication.) 3 × 5 × 2 can be found by 3 × 5 = 15, then 15 × 2 = 30, or by 5 × 2 = 10, then 3 × 10 = 30. (Associative property of multiplication.) Knowing that 8 × 5 = 40 and 8 × 2 = 16, one can find 8 × 7 as 8 × (5 + 2) = (8 × 5) + (8 × 2) = 40 + 16 = 56. (Distributive property.) Instructional focus: Students reason about equal groups, arrays, factors, products, quotients, and unknown group sizes. Multiplication and division are connected inverse relationships. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.

translations.title: Represent Products as Areas PLC Activity

The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Relate area to the operations of multiplication and addition. a. Find the area of a rectangle with whole-number side lengths by tiling it, and show that the area is the same as would be found by multiplying the side lengths. b. Use tiling to show in a concrete case that the area of a rectangle with whole- number side lengths a and b + c is the sum of a × b and a × c. Use area models to represent the distributive property in mathematical reasoning. d. Recognize area as additive. Find areas of rectilinear figures by decomposing them into non-overlapping rectangles and adding the areas of the non- overlapping parts, applying this technique to solv e real world problems. Apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide.2 Examples: If 6 × 4 = 24 is known, then 4 × 6 = 24 is also known. translations.title: Addition and Subtraction Situations
translations.explanation: Addition and Subtraction Situations is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Wrapping Up Addition and Subtraction Within 1,000”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:3.NBT.A.2, CCSS:3.OA.D.9. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Fluently add and subtract within 1000 using strategies and algorithms based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction. Identify arithmetic patterns (including patterns in the addition table or multiplication table), and explain them using properties of operations. For example, observe that 4 times a number is always even, and explain why 4 times a number can be decomposed into two equal addends. 1See Glossary, Table 2. 2Students need not use formal terms for these properties. 3This standard is limited to problems posed with whole numbers and having whole-number an- swers; students should know how to perform operations in the conventional order when there are no parentheses to specify a particular order (Order of Operations). Instructional focus: Students use the base-ten structure to read, compose, decompose, compare, round, and calculate with whole numbers or decimals at the grade-appropriate level. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Addition and Subtraction Situations. A digit has a value determined by its position. Moving one place left multiplies place value by 10; moving one place right divides it by 10. Reliable algorithms preserve place value by aligning like units and regrouping only when needed.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: The number 862 has 8 hundreds, 6 tens, and 2 ones, so 862 = 800 + 60 + 2. Adding 41 gives 862 + 41 = 903. Example 2: The number 577 has 5 hundreds, 7 tens, and 7 ones, so 577 = 500 + 70 + 7. Adding 58 gives 577 + 58 = 635.

Step 4: the sum is 903; estimate 862+about 41 to confirm the magnitude. Step 1: decompose 577 by place value. Step 2: decompose 58 if helpful. translations.title: Analyze Subtraction Algorithms
translations.explanation: Analyze Subtraction Algorithms is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Wrapping Up Addition and Subtraction Within 1,000”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:3.NBT.A.2. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Fluently add and subtract within 1000 using strategies and algorithms based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction. Instructional focus: Students use the base-ten structure to read, compose, decompose, compare, round, and calculate with whole numbers or decimals at the grade-appropriate level. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Analyze Subtraction Algorithms. A digit has a value determined by its position. Moving one place left multiplies place value by 10; moving one place right divides it by 10. Reliable algorithms preserve place value by aligning like units and regrouping only when needed.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: The number 596 has 5 hundreds, 9 tens, and 6 ones, so 596 = 500 + 90 + 6. Adding 31 gives 596 + 31 = 627. Example 2: The number 349 has 3 hundreds, 4 tens, and 9 ones, so 349 = 300 + 40 + 9. Adding 61 gives 349 + 61 = 410.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: decompose 596 by place value. Step 2: decompose 31 if helpful. Step 3: combine like place-value units and regroup when ten of a unit are formed. Step 4: the sum is 627; estimate 596+about 31 to confirm the magnitude. Step 1: decompose 349 by place value. Step 2: decompose 61 if helpful. Step 3: combine like place-value units and regroup when ten of a unit are formed. Step 4: the sum is 410; estimate 349+about 61 to confirm the magnitude.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Analyze Subtraction Algorithms. Do not compare numbers by looking at only one digit. Keep place values aligned in written calculations, especially with decimals. Estimate before or after computing so that misplaced digits and unreasonable answers are detected.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Analyze Subtraction Algorithms. Use place value to represent the number, select an efficient operation or comparison strategy, and verify the magnitude of the result.

translations.title: Subtract Strategically
translations.explanation: Subtract Strategically is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Wrapping Up Addition and Subtraction Within 1,000”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:3.NBT.A.2, CCSS:3.OA.B.5. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Fluently add and subtract within 1000 using strategies and algorithms based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction. Apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide.2 Examples: If 6 × 4 = 24 is known, then 4 × 6 = 24 is also known. (Commutative property of multiplication.) 3 × 5 × 2 can be found by 3 × 5 = 15, then 15 × 2 = 30, or by 5 × 2 = 10, then 3 × 10 = 30. (Associative property of multiplication.) Knowing that 8 × 5 = 40 and 8 × 2 = 16, one can find 8 × 7 as 8 × (5 + 2) = (8 × 5) + (8 × 2) = 40 + 16 = 56. (Distributive property.) translations.title: Round and Round Again
translations.explanation: Round and Round Again is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Wrapping Up Addition and Subtraction Within 1,000”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:3.NBT.A.1, CCSS:3.OA.C.7. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Use place value understanding to round whole numbers to the nearest 10 or 100. Fluently multiply and divide within 100, using strategies such as the relationship between multiplication and division (e.g., knowing that 8 × 5 = 40, one knows 40 ÷ 5 = 8) or properties of operations. By the end of Grade 3, know from memory all products of two one-digit numbers. Instructional focus: Students use the base-ten structure to read, compose, decompose, compare, round, and calculate with whole numbers or decimals at the grade-appropriate level. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Round and Round Again. A digit has a value determined by its position. Moving one place left multiplies place value by 10; moving one place right divides it by 10. Reliable algorithms preserve place value by aligning like units and regrouping only when needed.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: The number 285 has 2 hundreds, 8 tens, and 5 ones, so 285 = 200 + 80 + 5. Adding 36 gives 285 + 36 = 321. Example 2: The number 222 has 2 hundreds, 2 tens, and 2 ones, so 222 = 200 + 20 + 2. Adding 13 gives 222 + 13 = 235.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: decompose 285 by place value. Step 2: decompose 36 if helpful. Step 3: combine like place-value units and regroup when ten of a unit are formed. Step 4: the sum is 321; estimate 285+about 36 to confirm the magnitude. Step 1: decompose 222 by place value. Step 2: decompose 13 if helpful. Step 3: combine like place-value units and regroup when ten of a unit are formed. Step 4: the sum is 235; estimate 222+about 13 to confirm the magnitude.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Round and Round Again. Do not compare numbers by looking at only one digit. Keep place values aligned in written calculations, especially with decimals. Estimate before or after computing so that misplaced digits and unreasonable answers are detected.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Round and Round Again. Use place value to represent the number, select an efficient operation or comparison strategy, and verify the magnitude of the result.

translations.title: Does It Make Sense? PLC Activity
translations.explanation: Does It Make Sense? PLC Activity is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Wrapping Up Addition and Subtraction Within 1,000”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:3.OA.D.8. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Solve two-step word problems using the four operations. Represent these problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity. Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding.3 Instructional focus: Students reason about equal groups, arrays, factors, products, quotients, and unknown group sizes. Multiplication and division are connected inverse relationships. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Does It Make Sense? PLC Activity. A product can represent equal groups or rows and columns. Division can ask how many groups or how many objects are in each group. Factor pairs describe the same product, and multiplication can be checked with division.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Arrange 7 equal groups with 8 objects in each group. The product is 7 × 8 = 56; therefore 56 ÷ 7 = 8. Example 2: Arrange 5 equal groups with 5 objects in each group. The product is 5 × 5 = 25; therefore 25 ÷ 5 = 5.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify 7 groups and 8 objects per group. Step 2: multiply 7 by 8 to get 56. Step 3: interpret 56 as the total. Step 4: check with the inverse relationship 56 ÷ 7 = 8. Step 1: identify 5 groups and 5 objects per group. Step 2: multiply 5 by 5 to get 25. Step 3: interpret 25 as the total. Step 4: check with the inverse relationship 25 ÷ 5 = 5.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Does It Make Sense? PLC Activity. Do not swap the meaning of number of groups and size of each group without checking the context. A remainder must be interpreted, not ignored automatically. Verify division by multiplying the quotient by the divisor when appropriate.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Does It Make Sense? PLC Activity. Model equal groups clearly, connect multiplication with division, compute accurately, and interpret the answer in context.

Tytuł i kolejność pochodzą z zaakceptowanego źródła pedagogicznego, natomiast granice merytoryczne wyznaczają oficjalne standardy Common Core.

Dzielenie może pytać o liczbę grup lub liczbę elementów w każdej grupie. Pary czynników dają ten sam iloczyn, a mnożenie można sprawdzić dzieleniem.
translations.workedExamples: Przykład 1: Ułóż 7 równych grup po 8 elementów. Iloczyn wynosi 7 × 8 = 56, więc 56 ÷ 7 = 8. Przykład 2: Ułóż 5 równych grup po 5 elementów. Iloczyn wynosi 5 × 5 = 25, więc 25 ÷ 5 = 5.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Krok 1: rozpoznaj 7 grup po 8 elementów. Krok 2: pomnóż 7 przez 8 i otrzymaj 56. Krok 3: zinterpretuj 56 jako całość. Krok 4: sprawdź działaniem odwrotnym 56 ÷ 7 = 8. Krok 1: rozpoznaj 5 grup po 5 elementów. Krok 2: pomnóż 5 przez 5 i otrzymaj 25. Krok 3: zinterpretuj 25 jako całość. Krok 4: sprawdź działaniem odwrotnym 25 ÷ 5 = 5.
translations.commonMistakes: Cel tej lekcji: Mnożenie i dzielenie — Does It Make Sense? PLC Activity. Nie zamieniaj bez sprawdzenia liczby grup z liczbą elementów w grupie. Resztę z dzielenia trzeba zinterpretować, a nie automatycznie pominąć. Gdy to możliwe, sprawdzaj dzielenie za pomocą mnożenia.
translations.quickSummary: Cel tej lekcji: Mnożenie i dzielenie — Does It Make Sense? PLC Activity. Wyraźnie modeluj równe grupy, łącz mnożenie z dzieleniem, licz dokładnie i interpretuj wynik w kontekście.

translations.title: How Many Groups?
translations.explanation: How Many Groups? is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Relating Multiplication to Division”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:3.OA.A.2, CCSS:3.OA.A.3. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Interpret whole-number quotients of whole numbers, e.g., interpret 56 ÷ 8 as the number of objects in each share when 56 objects are partitioned equally into 8 shares, or as a number of shares when 56 objects are partitioned into equal shares of 8 objects each. For example, describe a context in which a number of shares or a number of groups can be expressed as 56 ÷ 8. Use multiplication and division within 100 to solve word problems in situations involving equal groups, arrays, and measurement quantities, e.g., by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.1 Instructional focus: Students reason about equal groups, arrays, factors, products, quotients, and unknown group sizes. Multiplication and division are connected inverse relationships. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: How Many Groups?. A product can represent equal groups or rows and columns. Division can ask how many groups or how many objects are in each group. Factor pairs describe the same product, and multiplication can be checked with division.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Arrange 6 equal groups with 7 objects in each group. The product is 6 × 7 = 42; therefore 42 ÷ 6 = 7. Example 2: Arrange 7 equal groups with 3 objects in each group. The product is 7 × 3 = 21; therefore 21 ÷ 7 = 3.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify 6 groups and 7 objects per group. Step 2: multiply 6 by 7 to get 42. Step 3: interpret 42 as the total. Step 4: check with the inverse relationship 42 ÷ 6 = 7. Step 1: identify 7 groups and 3 objects per group. Step 2: multiply 7 by 3 to get 21. Step 3: interpret 21 as the total. Step 4: check with the inverse relationship 21 ÷ 7 = 3.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: How Many Groups?. Do not swap the meaning of number of groups and size of each group without checking the context. A remainder must be interpreted, not ignored automatically. Verify division by multiplying the quotient by the divisor when appropriate.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: How Many Groups?. Model equal groups clearly, connect multiplication with division, compute accurately, and interpret the answer in context.

translations.title: Explore Multiplication Strategies with Rectangles
translations.explanation: Explore Multiplication Strategies with Rectangles is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Relating Multiplication to Division”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:3.MD.C.7, CCSS:3.OA.C.7. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Relate area to the operations of multiplication and addition. a. Find the area of a rectangle with whole-number side lengths by tiling it, and show that the area is the same as would be found by multiplying the side lengths. b. Multiply side lengths to find areas of rectangles with whole-number side lengths in the context of solving real world and mathematical problems, and represent whole-number products as rectangular areas in mathematical reasoning. c. Use tiling to show in a concrete case that the area of a rectangle with whole- number side lengths a and b + c is the sum of a × b and a × c. Use area models to represent the distributive property in mathematical reasoning. d. Recognize area as additive. Find areas of rectilinear figures by decomposing them into non-overlapping rectangles and adding the areas of the non- overlapping parts, applying this technique to solv e real world problems. Fluently multiply and divide within 100, using strategies such as the relationship between multiplication and division (e.g., knowing that 8 × 5 = 40, one knows 40 ÷ 5 = 8) or properties of operations. By the end of Grade 3, know from memory all products of two one-digit numbers. Instructional focus: Students connect measurable attributes with units, measurement procedures, representations of data, and calculations that answer a concrete question. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Explore Multiplication Strategies with Rectangles. Choose a unit that matches the attribute, use equal-size units without gaps or overlaps, record the unit with the number, and interpret tables, line plots, clocks, money, area, volume, or angle measures according to the problem.

translations.title: Multiply Multiples of Ten
translations.explanation: Multiply Multiples of Ten is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Relating Multiplication to Division”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:3.NBT.A.3. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Multiply one-digit whole numbers by multiples of 10 in the range 10–90 (e.g., 9 × 80, 5 × 60) using strategies based on place value and properties of operations. Instructional focus: Students use the base-ten structure to read, compose, decompose, compare, round, and calculate with whole numbers or decimals at the grade-appropriate level. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Multiply Multiples of Ten. A digit has a value determined by its position. Moving one place left multiplies place value by 10; moving one place right divides it by 10. Reliable algorithms preserve place value by aligning like units and regrouping only when needed.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: The number 318 has 3 hundreds, 1 tens, and 8 ones, so 318 = 300 + 10 + 8. Adding 48 gives 318 + 48 = 366. Example 2: The number 475 has 4 hundreds, 7 tens, and 5 ones, so 475 = 400 + 70 + 5. Adding 15 gives 475 + 15 = 490.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: decompose 318 by place value. Step 2: decompose 48 if helpful. Step 3: combine like place-value units and regroup when ten of a unit are formed. Step 4: the sum is 366; estimate 318+about 48 to confirm the magnitude. Step 1: decompose 475 by place value. Step 2: decompose 15 if helpful. Step 3: combine like place-value units and regroup when ten of a unit are formed. Step 4: the sum is 490; estimate 475+about 15 to confirm the magnitude.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Multiply Multiples of Ten. Do not compare numbers by looking at only one digit. Keep place values aligned in written calculations, especially with decimals. Estimate before or after computing so that misplaced digits and unreasonable answers are detected.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Multiply Multiples of Ten. Use place value to represent the number, select an efficient operation or comparison strategy, and verify the magnitude of the result.

translations.title: Solve Problems With Equal Groups
translations.explanation: Solve Problems With Equal Groups is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Relating Multiplication to Division”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:3.OA.A.3, CCSS:3.OA.B.5. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Use multiplication and division within 100 to solve word problems in situations involving equal groups, arrays, and measurement quantities, e.g., by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.1 Apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide.2 Examples: If 6 × 4 = 24 is known, then 4 × 6 = 24 is also known. (Commutative property of multiplication.) 3 × 5 × 2 can be found by 3 × 5 = 15, then 15 × 2 = 30, or by 5 × 2 = 10, then 3 × 10 = 30. (Associative property of multiplication.) Knowing that 8 × 5 = 40 and 8 × 2 = 16, one can find 8 × 7 as 8 × (5 + 2) = (8 × 5) + (8 × 2) = 40 + 16 = 56. (Distributive property.) Instructional focus: Students reason about equal groups, arrays, factors, products, quotients, and unknown group sizes. Multiplication and division are connected inverse relationships. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Solve Problems With Equal Groups. A product can represent equal groups or rows and columns. Division can ask how many groups or how many objects are in each group. Factor pairs describe the same product, and multiplication can be checked with division.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Arrange 4 equal groups with 2 objects in each group. The product is 4 × 2 = 8; therefore 8 ÷ 4 = 2. Example 2: Arrange 9 equal groups with 3 objects in each group. The product is 9 × 3 = 27; therefore 27 ÷ 9 = 3.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify 4 groups and 2 objects per group. Step 2: multiply 4 by 2 to get 8. Step 3: interpret 8 as the total. Step 4: check with the inverse relationship 8 ÷ 4 = 2. Step 1: identify 9 groups and 3 objects per group. Step 2: multiply 9 by 3 to get 27. Step 3: interpret 27 as the total. Step 4: check with the inverse relationship 27 ÷ 9 = 3.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Solve Problems With Equal Groups. Do not swap the meaning of number of groups and size of each group without checking the context. A remainder must be interpreted, not ignored automatically. Verify division by multiplying the quotient by the divisor when appropriate.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Solve Problems With Equal Groups. Model equal groups clearly, connect multiplication with division, compute accurately, and interpret the answer in context.

Krok 1: rozpoznaj 9 grup po 3 elementów. Krok 2: pomnóż 9 przez 3 i otrzymaj 27. Krok 3: zinterpretuj 27 jako całość. Krok 4: sprawdź działaniem odwrotnym 27 ÷ 9 = 3.

translations.title: Name the Parts
translations.explanation: Name the Parts is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Fractions as Numbers”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:3.G.A.2, CCSS:3.NF.A.1. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Partition shapes into parts with equal areas. Express the area of each part as a unit fraction of the whole. For example, partition a shape into 4 parts with equal area, and describe the area of each part as 1/4 of the area of the shape. Understand a fraction 1/b as the quantity formed by 1 part when a whole is partitioned into b equal parts; understand a fraction a/b as the quantity formed by a parts of size 1/b. Instructional focus: Students describe, compose, decompose, compare, and reason about shapes using defining properties rather than appearance alone. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Name the Parts. Geometric claims should use properties such as sides, angles, parallel or perpendicular lines, symmetry, coordinates, congruence, similarity, or equal partitions as appropriate. A drawing is evidence only when its marked or known properties justify the conclusion.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: A rectangle with side lengths 6 and 7 has four right angles and opposite sides of equal length. Its area is 6 × 7 = 42 square units. Example 2: A rectangle with side lengths 6 and 7 has four right angles and opposite sides of equal length. Its area is 6 × 7 = 42 square units.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify defining properties: four sides and four right angles. Step 2: use the given side lengths 6 and 7. Step 3: multiply to obtain area 42. Step 4: note that rotating the rectangle would not change its defining properties. Step 1: identify defining properties: four sides and four right angles. Step 2: use the given side lengths 6 and 7. Step 3: multiply to obtain area 42. Step 4: note that rotating the rectangle would not change its defining properties.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Name the Parts. Do not classify a shape by orientation, color, or size when those are not defining attributes. Do not assume an angle or length from appearance; use the stated properties or calculate them.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Name the Parts. Name the relevant properties, represent the figure accurately, reason from those properties, and verify that the conclusion remains true when the picture changes orientation or scale.

translations.title: Name Parts as Fractions
translations.explanation: Name Parts as Fractions is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Fractions as Numbers”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:3.NF.A.1. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Understand a fraction 1/b as the quantity formed by 1 part when a whole is partitioned into b equal parts; understand a fraction a/b as the quantity formed by a parts of size 1/b. Instructional focus: Students interpret fractions as numbers and as relationships between equal parts and a whole, then use equivalent forms and operations only when their meaning is preserved. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Name Parts as Fractions. The denominator tells how many equal parts make one whole; the numerator counts those parts. Equivalent fractions name the same point or quantity. For addition and subtraction, units must be the same size; for multiplication or division, interpret what is being scaled or shared.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Add fractions with the same unit: 3/8 + 5/8 = 8/8. This equals 1/1 in simplest form. Example 2: Add fractions with the same unit: 2/4 + 3/4 = 5/4. This equals 5/4 in simplest form.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: both fractions count 8ths, so the unit is already common. Step 2: add the numerators: 3+5=8. Step 3: keep denominator 8. Step 4: simplify 8/8 to 1/1 and compare it with 1 for reasonableness. Step 1: both fractions count 4ths, so the unit is already common. Step 2: add the numerators: 2+3=5. Step 3: keep denominator 4. Step 4: simplify 5/4 to 5/4 and compare it with 1 for reasonableness.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Name Parts as Fractions. Do not add denominators when adding fractions. Do not cancel terms across addition. Always ask whether the fraction is less than, equal to, or greater than one when estimating the reasonableness of an answer.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Name Parts as Fractions. Identify the fractional unit, preserve equal-sized parts, use equivalence when needed, perform the operation, and check the size of the answer.

translations.title: Build Fractions from Unit Fractions
translations.explanation: Build Fractions from Unit Fractions is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Fractions as Numbers”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:3.NF.A.1, CCSS:3.OA.C.7. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Understand a fraction 1/b as the quantity formed by 1 part when a whole is partitioned into b equal parts; understand a fraction a/b as the quantity formed by a parts of size 1/b. Fluently multiply and divide within 100, using strategies such as the relationship between multiplication and division (e.g., knowing that 8 × 5 = 40, one knows 40 ÷ 5 = 8) or properties of operations. By the end of Grade 3, know from memory all products of two one-digit numbers. Instructional focus: Students interpret fractions as numbers and as relationships between equal parts and a whole, then use equivalent forms and operations only when their meaning is preserved. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Build Fractions from Unit Fractions. The denominator tells how many equal parts make one whole; the numerator counts those parts. Equivalent fractions name the same point or quantity. For addition and subtraction, units must be the same size; for multiplication or division, interpret what is being scaled or shared.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Add fractions with the same unit: 2/8 + 4/8 = 6/8. This equals 3/4 in simplest form. Example 2: Add fractions with the same unit: 8/9 + 7/9 = 15/9. This equals 5/3 in simplest form.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: both fractions count 8ths, so the unit is already common. Step 2: add the numerators: 2+4=6. Step 3: keep denominator 8. Step 4: simplify 6/8 to 3/4 and compare it with 1 for reasonableness. Step 1: both fractions count 9ths, so the unit is already common. Step 2: add the numerators: 8+7=15. Step 3: keep denominator 9. Step 4: simplify 15/9 to 5/3 and compare it with 1 for reasonableness.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Build Fractions from Unit Fractions. Do not add denominators when adding fractions. Do not cancel terms across addition. Always ask whether the fraction is less than, equal to, or greater than one when estimating the reasonableness of an answer.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Build Fractions from Unit Fractions. Identify the fractional unit, preserve equal-sized parts, use equivalence when needed, perform the operation, and check the size of the answer.

translations.title: Build Ułamki from Unit Ułamki
translations.explanation: Lekcja „Build Ułamki from Unit Ułamki” należy do działu „Fractions as Numbers” i jest dokładnie powiązana ze standardami CCSS:3.NF.A.1, CCSS:3.OA.C.7. Główny kierunek pracy: Uczeń interpretuje ułamki jako liczby oraz jako relację równych części do całości, a następnie stosuje ułamki równoważne i działania wtedy, gdy zachowane jest ich znaczenie. Tytuł i kolejność pochodzą z zaakceptowanego źródła pedagogicznego, natomiast granice merytoryczne wyznaczają oficjalne standardy Common Core.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Cel tej lekcji: Build Ułamki from Unit Ułamki. Mianownik mówi, na ile równych części podzielono całość, a licznik wskazuje liczbę takich części. Ułamki równoważne opisują tę samą liczbę. Przy dodawaniu i odejmowaniu części muszą mieć ten sam rozmiar; przy mnożeniu i dzieleniu trzeba interpretować skalowanie lub podział.
translations.workedExamples: Przykład 1: Dodaj ułamki o tej samej jednostce: 2/8 + 4/8 = 6/8. Po skróceniu otrzymujemy 3/4. Przykład 2: Dodaj ułamki o tej samej jednostce: 8/9 + 7/9 = 15/9. Po skróceniu otrzymujemy 5/3.

Krok 4: skróć 6/8 do 3/4 i porównaj wynik z 1. Krok 1: oba ułamki opisują części 1/9, więc jednostka jest wspólna. Krok 2: dodaj liczniki: 8+7=15. Krok 3: zachowaj mianownik 9. translations.title: To the Number Line
translations.explanation: To the Number Line is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Fractions as Numbers”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:3.NF.A.2. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Understand a fraction as a number on the number line; represent fractions on a number line diagram. a. Represent a fraction 1/b on a number line diagram by defining the interval from 0 to 1 as the whole and partitioning it into b equal parts. Recognize that each part has size 1/ b and that the endpoint of the part based at 0 locates the number 1/b on the number line. b. Represent a fraction a/b on a number line diagram by marking off a lengths 1/b from 0. Recognize that the resulting interval has size a/b and that its endpoint locates the number a/b on the number line. Instructional focus: Students interpret fractions as numbers and as relationships between equal parts and a whole, then use equivalent forms and operations only when their meaning is preserved. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.

translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Add fractions with the same unit: 2/8 + 5/8 = 7/8. This equals 7/8 in simplest form. Example 2: Add fractions with the same unit: 2/3 + 1/3 = 3/3. This equals 1/1 in simplest form.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: both fractions count 8ths, so the unit is already common. Step 2: add the numerators: 2+5=7. Step 3: keep denominator 8. Step 4: simplify 7/8 to 7/8 and compare it with 1 for reasonableness. Step 1: both fractions count 3ths, so the unit is already common. Step 2: add the numerators: 2+1=3. Step 3: keep denominator 3. Główny kierunek pracy: Uczeń łączy mierzalne cechy z jednostkami, sposobem wykonywania pomiaru, reprezentacją danych i obliczeniami odpowiadającymi na konkretne pytanie. Tytuł i kolejność pochodzą z zaakceptowanego źródła pedagogicznego, natomiast granice merytoryczne wyznaczają oficjalne standardy Common Core.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Cel tej lekcji: Pomiar i dane — Same Perimeter, Different Shapes. Dobierz jednostkę do mierzonej cechy, używaj jednostek jednakowej wielkości bez luk i nakładania, zapisuj jednostkę przy wyniku i interpretuj tabele, wykresy, czas, pieniądze, pole, objętość lub kąty zgodnie z zadaniem.
translations.workedExamples: Przykład 1: Prostokąt ma wymiary 3 na 8 jednostek. Pole wynosi 3 × 8 = 24 jednostek kwadratowych, a obwód 2(3+8) = 22 jednostek. Przykład 2: Prostokąt ma wymiary 4 na 2 jednostek. Pole wynosi 4 × 2 = 8 jednostek kwadratowych, a obwód 2(4+2) = 12 jednostek.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Krok 1: rozpoznaj mierzoną wielkość i jednostkę. Krok 2: pole: 3×8=24. Krok 3: obwód: 2(3+8)=22. Krok 4: przy polu zapisz jednostki kwadratowe, a przy obwodzie liniowe. Krok 1: rozpoznaj mierzoną wielkość i jednostkę. Krok 2: pole: 4×2=8. Krok 3: obwód: 2(4+2)=12. Krok 4: przy polu zapisz jednostki kwadratowe, a przy obwodzie liniowe.
translations.commonMistakes: Cel tej lekcji: Pomiar i dane — Same Perimeter, Different Shapes. Liczba bez jednostki może być niepełną odpowiedzią. Nie łącz różnych jednostek bez przeliczenia. Na wykresie najpierw sprawdź skalę i opisy; w geometrii odróżniaj długość, pole, miarę kąta i objętość.
translations.quickSummary: Cel tej lekcji: Pomiar i dane — Same Perimeter, Different Shapes. Ustal, co jest mierzone, prawidłowo dobierz lub przelicz jednostki, wykonaj obliczenie albo odczyt i podaj wynik z jednostką oraz znaczeniem.

translations.title: Find the Perimeter PLC Activity
translations.explanation: Find the Perimeter PLC Activity is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Two-dimensional Shapes and Perimeter”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:3.MD.D.8, CCSS:3.OA.C.7. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Solve real world and mathematical problems involving perimeters of polygons, including finding the perimeter given the side lengths, finding an unknown side length, and exhibiting rectangles with the same perimeter and different areas or with the same area and different perimeters. Fluently multiply and divide within 100, using strategies such as the relationship between multiplication and division (e.g., knowing that 8 × 5 = 40, one knows 40 ÷ 5 = 8) or properties of operations. By the end of Grade 3, know from memory all products of two one-digit numbers. Instructional focus: Students connect measurable attributes with units, measurement procedures, representations of data, and calculations that answer a concrete question. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Find the Perimeter PLC Activity. Choose a unit that matches the attribute, use equal-size units without gaps or overlaps, record the unit with the number, and interpret tables, line plots, clocks, money, area, volume, or angle measures according to the problem.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: A rectangle measures 11 units by 4 units. Its area is 11 × 4 = 44 square units, while its perimeter is 2(11+4) = 30 units. Example 2: A rectangle measures 12 units by 7 units. Its area is 12 × 7 = 84 square units, while its perimeter is 2(12+7) = 38 units.

Step 4: attach square units to area and linear units to perimeter. Step 1: identify the requested attribute and units. Step 2: for area, multiply length by width: 12×7=84. translations.title: Problem Solving With Perimeter and Area
translations.explanation: Problem Solving With Perimeter and Area is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Two-dimensional Shapes and Perimeter”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:3.MD.D.8, CCSS:3.OA.C.7, CCSS:3.OA.D.8. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Solve real world and mathematical problems involving perimeters of polygons, including finding the perimeter given the side lengths, finding an unknown side length, and exhibiting rectangles with the same perimeter and different areas or with the same area and different perimeters. Fluently multiply and divide within 100, using strategies such as the relationship between multiplication and division (e.g., knowing that 8 × 5 = 40, one knows 40 ÷ 5 = 8) or properties of operations. By the end of Grade 3, know from memory all products of two one-digit numbers. Solve two-step word problems using the four operations. Represent these problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity. Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding.3 Instructional focus: Students reason about equal groups, arrays, factors, products, quotients, and unknown group sizes. Multiplication and division are connected inverse relationships. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Problem Solving With Perimeter and Area. A product can represent equal groups or rows and columns. Division can ask how many groups or how many objects are in each group. Factor pairs describe the same product, and multiplication can be checked with division.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Arrange 7 equal groups with 4 objects in each group. The product is 7 × 4 = 28; therefore 28 ÷ 7 = 4. Example 2: Arrange 5 equal groups with 2 objects in each group. The product is 5 × 2 = 10; therefore 10 ÷ 5 = 2.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify 7 groups and 4 objects per group. Step 2: multiply 7 by 4 to get 28. Step 3: interpret 28 as the total. Step 4: check with the inverse relationship 28 ÷ 7 = 4. Step 1: identify 5 groups and 2 objects per group. Step 2: multiply 5 by 2 to get 10. Step 3: interpret 10 as the total. Step 4: check with the inverse relationship 10 ÷ 5 = 2.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Problem Solving With Perimeter and Area. Do not swap the meaning of number of groups and size of each group without checking the context. A remainder must be interpreted, not ignored automatically. Verify division by multiplying the quotient by the divisor when appropriate.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Problem Solving With Perimeter and Area. Model equal groups clearly, connect multiplication with division, compute accurately, and interpret the answer in context.

translations.title: Problem Solving With Perimeter and Pole
translations.explanation: Lekcja „Problem Solving With Perimeter and Pole” należy do działu „Two-dimensional Shapes and Perimeter” i jest dokładnie powiązana ze standardami CCSS:3.MD.D.8, CCSS:3.OA.C.7, CCSS:3.OA.D.8. Główny kierunek pracy: Uczeń rozumuje o równych grupach, tablicach, czynnikach, iloczynach, ilorazach i nieznanej wielkości grupy. Mnożenie i dzielenie są działaniami wzajemnie odwrotnymi. Tytuł i kolejność pochodzą z zaakceptowanego źródła pedagogicznego, natomiast granice merytoryczne wyznaczają oficjalne standardy Common Core.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Cel tej lekcji: Problem Solving With Perimeter and Pole. Iloczyn może opisywać równe grupy albo układ w wierszach i kolumnach. Dzielenie może pytać o liczbę grup lub liczbę elementów w każdej grupie. Pary czynników dają ten sam iloczyn, a mnożenie można sprawdzić dzieleniem.
translations.workedExamples: Przykład 1: Ułóż 7 równych grup po 4 elementów. Iloczyn wynosi 7 × 4 = 28, więc 28 ÷ 7 = 4. Przykład 2: Ułóż 5 równych grup po 2 elementów. Iloczyn wynosi 5 × 2 = 10, więc 10 ÷ 5 = 2.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Krok 1: rozpoznaj 7 grup po 4 elementów. Krok 2: pomnóż 7 przez 4 i otrzymaj 28. Krok 3: zinterpretuj 28 jako całość. Krok 4: sprawdź działaniem odwrotnym 28 ÷ 7 = 4. Krok 1: rozpoznaj 5 grup po 2 elementów. Krok 2: pomnóż 5 przez 2 i otrzymaj 10. Krok 3: zinterpretuj 10 jako całość. Krok 4: sprawdź działaniem odwrotnym 10 ÷ 5 = 2.
translations.commonMistakes: Cel tej lekcji: Problem Solving With Perimeter and Pole. Nie zamieniaj bez sprawdzenia liczby grup z liczbą elementów w grupie. Resztę z dzielenia trzeba zinterpretować, a nie automatycznie pominąć. Gdy to możliwe, sprawdzaj dzielenie za pomocą mnożenia.
translations.quickSummary: Cel tej lekcji: Problem Solving With Perimeter and Pole. Wyraźnie modeluj równe grupy, łącz mnożenie z dzieleniem, licz dokładnie i interpretuj wynik w kontekście.

translations.title: Estimation Explorations with Fractions
translations.explanation: Estimation Explorations with Fractions is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Putting It All Together”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:3.NF.A.1, CCSS:3.NF.A.2. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Understand a fraction 1/b as the quantity formed by 1 part when a whole is partitioned into b equal parts; understand a fraction a/b as the quantity formed by a parts of size 1/b. Understand a fraction as a number on the number line; represent fractions on a number line diagram. a. Represent a fraction 1/b on a number line diagram by defining the interval from 0 to 1 as the whole and partitioning it into b equal parts. Recognize that each part has size 1/ b and that the endpoint of the part based at 0 locates the number 1/b on the number line. b. Represent a fraction a/b on a number line diagram by marking off a lengths 1/b from 0. Recognize that the resulting interval has size a/b and that its endpoint locates the number a/b on the number line. Instructional focus: Students interpret fractions as numbers and as relationships between equal parts and a whole, then use equivalent forms and operations only when their meaning is preserved. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Estimation Explorations with Fractions. The denominator tells how many equal parts make one whole; the numerator counts those parts. Equivalent fractions name the same point or quantity. For addition and subtraction, units must be the same size; for multiplication or division, interpret what is being scaled or shared.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Add fractions with the same unit: 1/7 + 1/7 = 2/7. This equals 2/7 in simplest form. Example 2: Add fractions with the same unit: 2/3 + 2/3 = 4/3. This equals 4/3 in simplest form.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: both fractions count 7ths, so the unit is already common. Step 2: add the numerators: 1+1=2. Step 3: keep denominator 7. Step 4: simplify 2/7 to 2/7 and compare it with 1 for reasonableness. Step 1: both fractions count 3ths, so the unit is already common. Step 2: add the numerators: 2+2=4. Step 3: keep denominator 3. Step 4: simplify 4/3 to 4/3 and compare it with 1 for reasonableness.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Estimation Explorations with Fractions. Do not add denominators when adding fractions. Do not cancel terms across addition. Always ask whether the fraction is less than, equal to, or greater than one when estimating the reasonableness of an answer.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Estimation Explorations with Fractions. Identify the fractional unit, preserve equal-sized parts, use equivalence when needed, perform the operation, and check the size of the answer.

translations.title: Fractions Round Table PLC Activity
translations.explanation: Fractions Round Table PLC Activity is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Putting It All Together”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:3.NF.A.1, CCSS:3.NF.A.2, CCSS:3.NF.A.3. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Understand a fraction 1/b as the quantity formed by 1 part when a whole is partitioned into b equal parts; understand a fraction a/b as the quantity formed by a parts of size 1/b. Understand a fraction as a number on the number line; represent fractions on a number line diagram. a. Represent a fraction 1/b on a number line diagram by defining the interval from 0 to 1 as the whole and partitioning it into b equal parts. Recognize that each part has size 1/ b and that the endpoint of the part based at 0 locates the number 1/b on the number line. b. Represent a fraction a/b on a number line diagram by marking off a lengths 1/b from 0. Recognize that the resulting interval has size a/b and that its endpoint locates the number a/b on the number line. Explain equivalence of fractions in special cases, and compare fractions by reasoning about their size. a. Understand two fractions as equivalent (equal) if they are the same size, or the same point on a number line. b. Recognize and generate simple equivalent fractions, e.g., 1/2 = 2/4, 4/6 = 2/3). Explain why the fractions are equivalent, e.g., by using a visual fraction model. c. Express whole numbers as fractions, and recognize fractions that are equivalent to whole numbers. Examples: Express 3 in the form 3 = 3/1; recognize that 6/1 = 6; locate 4/4 and 1 at the same point of a number line diagram. d. Compare two fractions with t... Instructional focus: Students interpret fractions as numbers and as relationships between equal parts and a whole, then use equivalent forms and operations only when their meaning is preserved. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Fractions Round Table PLC Activity. The denominator tells how many equal parts make one whole; the numerator counts those parts. Equivalent fractions name the same point or quantity. For addition and subtraction, units must be the same size; for multiplication or division, interpret what is being scaled or shared.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Add fractions with the same unit: 1/3 + 1/3 = 2/3. This equals 2/3 in simplest form. Example 2: Add fractions with the same unit: 5/6 + 3/6 = 8/6. This equals 4/3 in simplest form.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: both fractions count 3ths, so the unit is already common. Step 2: add the numerators: 1+1=2. Step 3: keep denominator 3. Step 4: simplify 2/3 to 2/3 and compare it with 1 for reasonableness. Step 1: both fractions count 6ths, so the unit is already common. Step 2: add the numerators: 5+3=8. Step 3: keep denominator 6. Step 4: simplify 8/6 to 4/3 and compare it with 1 for reasonableness.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Fractions Round Table PLC Activity. Do not add denominators when adding fractions. Do not cancel terms across addition. Always ask whether the fraction is less than, equal to, or greater than one when estimating the reasonableness of an answer.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Fractions Round Table PLC Activity. Identify the fractional unit, preserve equal-sized parts, use equivalence when needed, perform the operation, and check the size of the answer.

Krok 4: skróć 2/3 do 2/3 i porównaj wynik z 1. Krok 1: oba ułamki opisują części 1/6, więc jednostka jest wspólna. Krok 2: dodaj liczniki: 5+3=8. Krok 3: zachowaj mianownik 6. Krok 4: skróć 8/6 do 4/3 i porównaj wynik z 1.

translations.title: Tiny House: Design and Solve PLC Activity
translations.explanation: Tiny House: Design and Solve PLC Activity is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Putting It All Together”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:3.MD.C.7, CCSS:3.MD.D.8. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Relate area to the operations of multiplication and addition. a. Find the area of a rectangle with whole-number side lengths by tiling it, and show that the area is the same as would be found by multiplying the side lengths. b. Multiply side lengths to find areas of rectangles with whole-number side lengths in the context of solving real world and mathematical problems, and represent whole-number products as rectangular areas in mathematical reasoning. c. Use tiling to show in a concrete case that the area of a rectangle with whole- number side lengths a and b + c is the sum of a × b and a × c. Use area models to represent the distributive property in mathematical reasoning. d. Recognize area as additive. Find areas of rectilinear figures by decomposing them into non-overlapping rectangles and adding the areas of the non- overlapping parts, applying this technique to solv e real world problems. Solve real world and mathematical problems involving perimeters of polygons, including finding the perimeter given the side lengths, finding an unknown side length, and exhibiting rectangles with the same perimeter and different areas or with the same area and different perimeters. Instructional focus: Students connect measurable attributes with units, measurement procedures, representations of data, and calculations that answer a concrete question. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Tiny House: Design and Solve PLC Activity. Choose a unit that matches the attribute, use equal-size units without gaps or overlaps, record the unit with the number, and interpret tables, line plots, clocks, money, area, volume, or angle measures according to the problem.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: A rectangle measures 12 units by 9 units. Its area is 12 × 9 = 108 square units, while its perimeter is 2(12+9) = 42 units. Example 2: A rectangle measures 11 units by 3 units. Its area is 11 × 3 = 33 square units, while its perimeter is 2(11+3) = 28 units.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify the requested attribute and units. Step 2: for area, multiply length by width: 12×9=108. Step 3: for perimeter, add all side lengths: 2(12+9)=42. Step 4: attach square units to area and linear units to perimeter. Step 1: identify the requested attribute and units. Step 2: for area, multiply length by width: 11×3=33. Step 3: for perimeter, add all side lengths: 2(11+3)=28. Step 4: attach square units to area and linear units to perimeter.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Tiny House: Design and Solve PLC Activity. A number without its unit can be incomplete. Do not mix incompatible units before converting them. In graphs, read the scale and labels before drawing conclusions; in geometric measurement, distinguish length, area, angle, and volume.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Tiny House: Design and Solve PLC Activity. Identify what is measured, choose or convert units correctly, calculate or read the representation, and state the result with its unit and meaning.

translations.title: Tiny House: Design and Rozwiązywanie PLC Activity

Główny kierunek pracy: Uczeń łączy mierzalne cechy z jednostkami, sposobem wykonywania pomiaru, reprezentacją danych i obliczeniami odpowiadającymi na konkretne pytanie. Tytuł i kolejność pochodzą z zaakceptowanego źródła pedagogicznego, natomiast granice merytoryczne wyznaczają oficjalne standardy Common Core.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Cel tej lekcji: Tiny House: Design and Rozwiązywanie PLC Activity. Dobierz jednostkę do mierzonej cechy, używaj jednostek jednakowej wielkości bez luk i nakładania, zapisuj jednostkę przy wyniku i interpretuj tabele, wykresy, czas, pieniądze, pole, objętość lub kąty zgodnie z zadaniem.

translations.stepByStepSolutions: Krok 1: rozpoznaj mierzoną wielkość i jednostkę. Krok 2: pole: 12×9=108. Krok 3: obwód: 2(12+9)=42. Krok 4: przy polu zapisz jednostki kwadratowe, a przy obwodzie liniowe. Krok 1: rozpoznaj mierzoną wielkość i jednostkę. Krok 2: pole: 11×3=33. Krok 3: obwód: 2(11+3)=28. Krok 4: przy polu zapisz jednostki kwadratowe, a przy obwodzie liniowe.

translations.title: Tiny House: Cost
translations.explanation: Tiny House: Cost is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Putting It All Together”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:3.NBT.A.2, CCSS:3.OA.D.8. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Fluently add and subtract within 1000 using strategies and algorithms based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction. Solve two-step word problems using the four operations. Represent these problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity. Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding.3 Instructional focus: Students use the base-ten structure to read, compose, decompose, compare, round, and calculate with whole numbers or decimals at the grade-appropriate level. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Tiny House: Cost. A digit has a value determined by its position. Moving one place left multiplies place value by 10; moving one place right divides it by 10. Reliable algorithms preserve place value by aligning like units and regrouping only when needed.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: The number 574 has 5 hundreds, 7 tens, and 4 ones, so 574 = 500 + 70 + 4. Adding 49 gives 574 + 49 = 623. Example 2: The number 813 has 8 hundreds, 1 tens, and 3 ones, so 813 = 800 + 10 + 3. Adding 66 gives 813 + 66 = 879.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: decompose 574 by place value. Step 2: decompose 49 if helpful. Step 3: combine like place-value units and regroup when ten of a unit are formed. Step 4: the sum is 623; estimate 574+about 49 to confirm the magnitude. Step 1: decompose 813 by place value. Step 2: decompose 66 if helpful. Step 3: combine like place-value units and regroup when ten of a unit are formed. Step 4: the sum is 879; estimate 813+about 66 to confirm the magnitude.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Tiny House: Cost. Do not compare numbers by looking at only one digit. Keep place values aligned in written calculations, especially with decimals. Estimate before or after computing so that misplaced digits and unreasonable answers are detected.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Tiny House: Cost. Use place value to represent the number, select an efficient operation or comparison strategy, and verify the magnitude of the result.

Przesunięcie o jedno miejsce w lewo mnoży wartość pozycyjną przez 10, a w prawo dzieli ją przez 10. translations.stepByStepSolutions: Krok 1: rozłóż 574 według wartości pozycyjnych. Krok 2: w razie potrzeby rozłóż 49. Krok 3: połącz te same rzędy i przegrupuj dziesięć jednostek w jednostkę wyższego rzędu. Krok 4: wynik to 623; oszacuj, aby sprawdzić jego wielkość. Krok 1: rozłóż 813 według wartości pozycyjnych. Krok 2: w razie potrzeby rozłóż 66. Krok 3: połącz te same rzędy i przegrupuj dziesięć jednostek w jednostkę wyższego rzędu. Krok 4: wynik to 879; oszacuj, aby sprawdzić jego wielkość.
translations.commonMistakes: Cel tej lekcji: Wartość pozycyjna i działania w systemie dziesiętnym — Tiny House: Cost. Nie porównuj liczb na podstawie jednej cyfry. W zapisie działań ustawiaj te same wartości pozycyjne pod sobą, szczególnie przy liczbach dziesiętnych. Szacuj wynik, aby wykrywać przesunięte cyfry i nierozsądne odpowiedzi.
translations.quickSummary: Cel tej lekcji: Wartość pozycyjna i działania w systemie dziesiętnym — Tiny House: Cost. Wykorzystaj wartość pozycyjną do przedstawienia liczby, wybierz skuteczną strategię działania lub porównania i sprawdź wielkość wyniku.

translations.title: Multiplication Center Day
translations.explanation: Multiplication Center Day is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Putting It All Together”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:3.OA.C.7. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Fluently multiply and divide within 100, using strategies such as the relationship between multiplication and division (e.g., knowing that 8 × 5 = 40, one knows 40 ÷ 5 = 8) or properties of operations. By the end of Grade 3, know from memory all products of two one-digit numbers. Instructional focus: Students reason about equal groups, arrays, factors, products, quotients, and unknown group sizes. Multiplication and division are connected inverse relationships. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Multiplication Center Day. A product can represent equal groups or rows and columns. Division can ask how many groups or how many objects are in each group. Factor pairs describe the same product, and multiplication can be checked with division.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Arrange 5 equal groups with 3 objects in each group. The product is 5 × 3 = 15; therefore 15 ÷ 5 = 3. Example 2: Arrange 4 equal groups with 3 objects in each group. The product is 4 × 3 = 12; therefore 12 ÷ 4 = 3.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify 5 groups and 3 objects per group. Step 2: multiply 5 by 3 to get 15. Step 3: interpret 15 as the total. Step 4: check with the inverse relationship 15 ÷ 5 = 3. Step 1: identify 4 groups and 3 objects per group. Step 2: multiply 4 by 3 to get 12. Step 3: interpret 12 as the total. Step 4: check with the inverse relationship 12 ÷ 4 = 3.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Multiplication Center Day. Do not swap the meaning of number of groups and size of each group without checking the context. A remainder must be interpreted, not ignored automatically. Verify division by multiplying the quotient by the divisor when appropriate.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Multiplication Center Day. Model equal groups clearly, connect multiplication with division, compute accurately, and interpret the answer in context.

translations.title: Mnożenie Center Day
translations.explanation: Lekcja „Mnożenie Center Day” należy do działu „Putting It All Together” i jest dokładnie powiązana ze standardami CCSS:3.OA.C.7. Główny kierunek pracy: Uczeń rozumuje o równych grupach, tablicach, czynnikach, iloczynach, ilorazach i nieznanej wielkości grupy. Mnożenie i dzielenie są działaniami wzajemnie odwrotnymi. Tytuł i kolejność pochodzą z zaakceptowanego źródła pedagogicznego, natomiast granice merytoryczne wyznaczają oficjalne standardy Common Core.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Cel tej lekcji: Mnożenie Center Day. Iloczyn może opisywać równe grupy albo układ w wierszach i kolumnach. Dzielenie może pytać o liczbę grup lub liczbę elementów w każdej grupie. Pary czynników dają ten sam iloczyn, a mnożenie można sprawdzić dzieleniem.
translations.workedExamples: Przykład 1: Ułóż 5 równych grup po 3 elementów. Iloczyn wynosi 5 × 3 = 15, więc 15 ÷ 5 = 3. Przykład 2: Ułóż 4 równych grup po 3 elementów. Iloczyn wynosi 4 × 3 = 12, więc 12 ÷ 4 = 3.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Krok 1: rozpoznaj 5 grup po 3 elementów. Krok 2: pomnóż 5 przez 3 i otrzymaj 15. Krok 3: zinterpretuj 15 jako całość. Krok 4: sprawdź działaniem odwrotnym 15 ÷ 5 = 3. Krok 1: rozpoznaj 4 grup po 3 elementów. Krok 2: pomnóż 4 przez 3 i otrzymaj 12. Krok 3: zinterpretuj 12 jako całość. translations.title: Estimation Exploration
translations.explanation: Estimation Exploration is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Putting It All Together”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:3.MD.B.4. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Generate measurement data by measuring lengths using rulers marked with halves and fourths of an inch. Show the data by making a line plot, where the horizontal scale is marked off in appropriate units—whole numbers, halves, or quarters. Instructional focus: Students connect measurable attributes with units, measurement procedures, representations of data, and calculations that answer a concrete question. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Estimation Exploration. Choose a unit that matches the attribute, use equal-size units without gaps or overlaps, record the unit with the number, and interpret tables, line plots, clocks, money, area, volume, or angle measures according to the problem.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: A rectangle measures 12 units by 7 units. Its area is 12 × 7 = 84 square units, while its perimeter is 2(12+7) = 38 units. Example 2: A rectangle measures 6 units by 7 units. Its area is 6 × 7 = 42 square units, while its perimeter is 2(6+7) = 26 units.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify the requested attribute and units. Step 2: for area, multiply length by width: 12×7=84. Step 3: for perimeter, add all side lengths: 2(12+7)=38. Step 4: attach square units to area and linear units to perimeter. Step 1: identify the requested attribute and units. Step 2: for area, multiply length by width: 6×7=42. Step 3: for perimeter, add all side lengths: 2(6+7)=26. Step 4: attach square units to area and linear units to perimeter.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Estimation Exploration. A number without its unit can be incomplete. Do not mix incompatible units before converting them. In graphs, read the scale and labels before drawing conclusions; in geometric measurement, distinguish length, area, angle, and volume.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Estimation Exploration. Identify what is measured, choose or convert units correctly, calculate or read the representation, and state the result with its unit and meaning.

translations.title: Number Talk
translations.explanation: Number Talk is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Putting It All Together”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:3.NBT.A.2. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Fluently add and subtract within 1000 using strategies and algorithms based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction. Instructional focus: Students use the base-ten structure to read, compose, decompose, compare, round, and calculate with whole numbers or decimals at the grade-appropriate level. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Number Talk. A digit has a value determined by its position. Moving one place left multiplies place value by 10; moving one place right divides it by 10. Reliable algorithms preserve place value by aligning like units and regrouping only when needed.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: The number 517 has 5 hundreds, 1 tens, and 7 ones, so 517 = 500 + 10 + 7. Adding 21 gives 517 + 21 = 538. Example 2: The number 755 has 7 hundreds, 5 tens, and 5 ones, so 755 = 700 + 50 + 5. Adding 14 gives 755 + 14 = 769.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: decompose 517 by place value. Step 2: decompose 21 if helpful. Step 3: combine like place-value units and regroup when ten of a unit are formed. Step 4: the sum is 538; estimate 517+about 21 to confirm the magnitude. Step 1: decompose 755 by place value. Step 2: decompose 14 if helpful. Step 3: combine like place-value units and regroup when ten of a unit are formed. Step 4: the sum is 769; estimate 755+about 14 to confirm the magnitude.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Number Talk. Do not compare numbers by looking at only one digit. Keep place values aligned in written calculations, especially with decimals. Estimate before or after computing so that misplaced digits and unreasonable answers are detected.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Number Talk. Use place value to represent the number, select an efficient operation or comparison strategy, and verify the magnitude of the result.

Główny kierunek pracy: Uczeń wykorzystuje strukturę systemu dziesiętnego do odczytywania, składania, rozkładania, porównywania, zaokrąglania i wykonywania działań na liczbach całkowitych lub dziesiętnych odpowiednio do poziomu. Poprawne algorytmy zachowują wartości pozycyjne przez ustawianie tych samych rzędów pod sobą i właściwe przegrupowanie.
translations.workedExamples: Przykład 1: Liczba 517 ma 5 setek, 1 dziesiątek i 7 jedności, więc 517 = 500 + 10 + 7. Po dodaniu 21 otrzymujemy 517 + 21 = 538. Przykład 2: Liczba 755 ma 7 setek, 5 dziesiątek i 5 jedności, więc 755 = 700 + 50 + 5. Po dodaniu 14 otrzymujemy 755 + 14 = 769.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Krok 1: rozłóż 517 według wartości pozycyjnych. Krok 2: w razie potrzeby rozłóż 21. Krok 3: połącz te same rzędy i przegrupuj dziesięć jednostek w jednostkę wyższego rzędu. Krok 4: wynik to 538; oszacuj, aby sprawdzić jego wielkość. Krok 1: rozłóż 755 według wartości pozycyjnych. Krok 2: w razie potrzeby rozłóż 14. Krok 3: połącz te same rzędy i przegrupuj dziesięć jednostek w jednostkę wyższego rzędu. Krok 4: wynik to 769; oszacuj, aby sprawdzić jego wielkość.
translations.commonMistakes: Cel tej lekcji: Liczba Talk. Nie porównuj liczb na podstawie jednej cyfry. W zapisie działań ustawiaj te same wartości pozycyjne pod sobą, szczególnie przy liczbach dziesiętnych. Szacuj wynik, aby wykrywać przesunięte cyfry i nierozsądne odpowiedzi.
translations.quickSummary: Cel tej lekcji: Liczba Talk. Wykorzystaj wartość pozycyjną do przedstawienia liczby, wybierz skuteczną strategię działania lub porównania i sprawdź wielkość wyniku.
